articles.title: Fever at home: when to see a doctor
articles.body: Most fevers settle in two to three days with rest, fluids and paracetamol at the right dose. See a doctor the same day if the fever is above 103°F (39.4°C), lasts more than three days, or comes with a stiff neck, rash, breathing difficulty, confusion or repeated vomiting. Children under three months with any fever need a doctor immediately.

articles.title: Five habits that keep blood pressure in check
articles.body: Cut back on salt (under one teaspoon a day across all food), walk briskly for 30 minutes on most days, keep alcohol low, sleep seven to eight hours, and check your BP at home once a week. If readings stay above 140/90, book a consultation: early treatment prevents heart and kidney damage.

articles.title: Living well with type 2 diabetes
articles.body: Fill half your plate with vegetables, a quarter with protein and a quarter with whole grains. Take medicines at the same time every day, check sugars as your doctor advised, and get an HbA1c test every three months. Inspect your feet daily for cuts or sores, and get an eye check every year.

articles.title: Monsoon infections: dengue, malaria and typhoid
articles.body: Stagnant water breeds mosquitoes, so empty coolers, pots and tyres weekly. Use repellent and full sleeves at dawn and dusk. Drink boiled or filtered water and avoid street food during the rains. A high fever with body ache, rash or bleeding gums needs a blood test the same day.

articles.title: Anxiety is common, and treatable
articles.body: Racing thoughts, poor sleep, a pounding heart and constant worry can all be anxiety. Regular exercise, limiting caffeine, slow breathing and talking to someone you trust help. If it affects work, study or relationships for more than two weeks, a psychiatrist or psychologist can help, and a video consultation is a private way to start.
